catalog_quote: § 5. Quantitative distinctions between vowels in modern Ossetic do not have phonemic significance. But formerly these distinctions were very essential and as the result of this past status, the modern vowels may be divided into two groups: strong: а е и о у; weak: æ ы. The former group can be traced back, as a rule, to the old long vowels or diphthongs; the latter, to the old short vowels. Even today the strong vowels remain somewhat longer. ... § 30. sweep_summary: Modern Ossetic is in the catalog as 'weight' (Abaev 1964 §5, §§30-31: stress on the first syllable if its vowel is strong, otherwise on the second). this search of works with stress in the title had two Glottolog items, which are one work: Cheung 1999, 'Some remarks on the history of the Ossetic accent', in van den Berg (ed.), Studies in Caucasian linguistics (Leiden: CNWS), 286-292 — the second item attributes it to the volume's editor and is a Glottolog duplicate. HAL holds the record (author's lab; one-line abstract, no file); HathiTrust has the volume search-only; Google Books, HathiTrust and the Leiden repository were blocked/could not be reached by automated download; OpenAlex/S2/CORE/archive.org gave nothing. The paper itself was not read (medium priority; diachronic, 7 pages; its fuller form is Cheung 2002:121ff, print/paywalled). While hunting it I found and read an open first-hand statement by the same author (Cheung 2008/2018, Nartamongæ XIII: 103-104, n.1 and n.13): historical (pre-)Ossetic had initial stress; the modern 'rhythmic-like' accent 'determined by the quantity/quality of the vowels' is secondary — this confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding and does not supersede Abaev 1964. Two paywalled reviews of the 1999 volume (Vajda, Language 77(2) 2001; Friedman, Studies in Language 25(2) 2001) and Schmitt's Kratylos 49 (2004) review of Cheung 2002 are low-priority leads.

new_statements.reading: The author of this search of works with stress in the title's only target paper states first-hand that modern Ossetic word accent is 'rhythmic-like' and 'determined by the quantity/quality of the vowels' (the strong/weak vowel distinction), i.e. the catalog's 'weight' coding, and that this is a secondary development from an older initial-stress system (his 1999 paper and 2002 book, pp. 121ff., argue the diachronic point). It confirms the catalog's synchronic coding without adding detail on the placement rule; it is a footnote in a paper on case morphology, so it does not displace Abaev 1964 as the deciding source.

new_statements.quote: 1. Ударение в осетинских словах может падать только на первый или второй слог. [...] 2. Если в первом слоге сильный гласный (а, е, и, о, у), a во втором слабый (ы, аэ), то ударение падает на первый слог. [...] Если в первом слоге слабый гласный, а во втором сильный, то ударение падает на второй слог. 3. Если в обоих первых слогах сильные гласные, то ударение падает чаще всего на первый слог. [...] 4. В словах и комплексах со слабыми гласными в обоих первых слогах ударение, как правило, падает на второй слог. [...] Все перечисленные выше правила позволяют охарактеризовать осетинское ударение как связанное, поскольку оно может падать только на первый или второй слог.
new_statements.translation: 1. Stress in Ossetic words can fall only on the first or the second syllable. [...] 2. If the first syllable has a strong vowel (a, e, i, o, u) and the second a weak one (y, æ), stress falls on the first syllable. [...] If the first syllable has a weak vowel and the second a strong one, stress falls on the second syllable. 3. If both of the first two syllables have strong vowels, stress most often falls on the first syllable. [...] 4. In words and complexes with weak vowels in both of the first two syllables, stress as a rule falls on the second syllable. [...] All the rules listed above allow Ossetic stress to be characterised as bound, since it can fall only on the first or the second syllable. (pp. 10-11; 'аэ' in the page text is the scanned rendering of æ)

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Ossetic has an empty rule field; this work supplies the rule. It agrees with the existing Cheung 2018 statement that the accent is 'rhythmic-like' and determined by the vowel quantity/quality (strong vs weak vowel) and adds the two-syllable window, the full case table, the definiteness shift, mobility under affixation, the exception lists and the instrumental measurements.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is confined to the first two syllables and its position is decided by vowel class (strong a, e, i, o, u vs weak y, æ): first syllable if it is strong and the second weak; second syllable if the first is weak and the second strong; both strong -> usually first; both weak -> usually second. Stress is mobile under affixation (a strong-vowel preverb takes the stress, e.g. fyss 'write!' -> b'afyss but ærf'yss) and shifts from the 2nd to the 1st syllable to mark definiteness (bæl'as 'a tree' vs b'ælas 'the tree'). The author's own summary (p. 23): Ossetic stress is 'связное, подвижное' (bound, mobile) and has culminative, delimitative, differentiating and constitutive functions. Instrumental part: stressed vowels are only 1.2x longer and 1.01x more intense than unstressed ones (weak contrast), yet native listeners locate the stress correctly (205 of 218 words), so the stress is weakly centred but culminative.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress beyond the second syllable only in Russian loanwords; lexical exceptions to rule 2 (ab'yræg 'abrek', xal'yvæ, agu'yvzæ 'glass', bas'ylyqq, iz'ær 'evening', Ir'yston 'Ossetia', etc.), to rule 3 (ir'on 'Ossetian', qab'aq, qat'ara, qaz'axxag, bab'a, nan'a, dad'a - mostly loans), and to rule 4 (initial-stressed zm'ælyn, s'ystyn, m'ysyn, r'æzyn, explained by a lost prothetic vowel; oblique forms of uyj; verbs with the prefix s-). In a recorded dictionary read by two normative speakers, 108 words got different stress from the two speakers (appendix, pp. 23-26); the 2002 orthographic dictionary marks stress wrongly. Minimal pairs by stress (after Bagaev): dzidz'a 'meat' / dz'idza 'wet-nurse', b'abyz 'duck' / Bab'yz (woman's name). In connected speech a word may lose its stress inside the syntagm (p. 22).
new_statements.identity_note: Both substantive works describe the Iron literary standard ('осетинский (иронский) литературный язык'); Akhvlediani 1963 cites Digor forms (imisun, iræzun; the article i-) only as historical evidence for Iron exceptions and the definiteness shift, and does not give a separate Digor stress rule here. Lyutikova & Tatevosov 2009 treat Iron syntax. Glottolog's osse1243 is the parent node; the catalog record 'Ossetic' therefore stands for Iron.

new_statements.quote: основной акцентологический закон современного осетинского языка сводится вкратце к следующему: ударение падает на первый слог, если он сильный, или на второй, если первый слабый. [...] В осетинском языке ударяется не каждое слово. Группы слов, определенным образом связанные синтаксически, объединяются под одно общее ударение, образуя так называемые акцентуальные единицы, или комплексы. [...] 1. Ударение может падать на первый или второй слог от начала, притом оно больше тяготеет ко второму слогу. 2. Если в первом слоге сильный гласный (а, о, е, у, и), а во втором — слабый (є, ы), то ударение падает ца первый слог.
new_statements.translation: the basic accentological law of modern Ossetic comes down briefly to this: stress falls on the first syllable if it is strong, or on the second if the first is weak. (p. 31) [...] In Ossetic not every word is stressed. Groups of words linked syntactically in a definite way are united under one common stress, forming so-called accentual units, or complexes. [...] 1. Stress may fall on the first or the second syllable from the beginning, and it gravitates more toward the second syllable. 2. If the first syllable has a strong vowel (a, o, e, u, i) and the second a weak one (æ, y), stress falls on the first syllable. (pp. 49-50; 'ца' is an scanned error for 'на', 'є' renders æ)

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the vowel-quality/weight reading in the existing Cheung 2018 statement and supplies the rule the empty catalog record lacks; adds the two-syllable window, the preference for the second syllable when both vowels are equal, the phrase-level domain (accentual complexes carry one stress), the definiteness shift and the exception classes. This is the primary source Dzakhova 2010 summarises.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on one of the first two syllables of the accentual unit (a word or a syntactically bound word group, which carries one stress): on the first syllable if its vowel is strong (a, o, e, u, i) and the second weak (æ, y); on the second if the first is weak and the second strong; both strong -> usually the first (especially when the first syllable is a strong-vowel preverb a-, ba-, ra-, or the second is a suffix/case ending, or in complexes); both weak -> as a rule the second. The historical comment (p. 31) frames this as the vowel-quantity legacy: the old quantitative distinction survives as strong vs weak vowels and decides the stress. Stress is termed dynamic/expiratory (§9) and Ossetic is said to have PHRASAL stress in the sense that rhythmic groups carry a single stress; the placement rules are the same for words and complexes. Shifting stress from the 2nd to the 1st syllable on nouns marks definiteness (functions as a definite article; explained historically from a lost Digor-type article i-).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the section treats accentual complexes with one stress each and 'logical stress' within the phrase (pp. 53-55).
new_statements.exceptions: (7) verbs with weak vowels in both first syllables but initial stress (mysyn, systyn, ræzyn) explained by a lost prothetic vowel (Digor imisun, istun, iræzun); (8) personal names usually stressed on the second syllable regardless of vowel class (Sozyryqo, Satana, Batyradz, Soslan, Sælimæt, Mæxæmæt, Tamaræ); many Russian loans (kommunist, bol'shevik, patriot) do not follow the rules; the definiteness shift (rule 6).
new_statements.identity_note: Both substantive works describe the Iron literary standard ('осетинский (иронский) литературный язык'); Akhvlediani 1963 cites Digor forms (imisun, iræzun; the article i-) only as historical evidence for Iron exceptions and the definiteness shift, and does not give a separate Digor stress rule here. Lyutikova & Tatevosov 2009 treat Iron syntax. Glottolog's osse1243 is the parent node; the catalog record 'Ossetic' therefore stands for Iron.

readall_conflicts: No substantive disagreement among the sources opened. Akhvlediani 1963 (§10, p. 49) adds that stress 'gravitates more toward the second syllable' and treats the stress domain as the phrase-level accentual complex (§9: Ossetic has 'фразовое ударение', groups of words carry one stress), whereas Dzakhova 2010 describes the same placement rules as word stress and notes only that a word may lose its stress inside a syntagm (p. 22); the two are compatible (Akhvlediani states the rules hold identically for words and complexes). Dzakhova's instrumental data show a weak acoustic contrast (1.2x duration, 1.01x intensity) and 108 words with speaker disagreement, which qualifies but does not overturn the rule. Cheung 1999 (not accessible) and Cheung 2018 (existing statement) concern the HISTORICAL accent (Cheung: initial; Kim: Sogdian-like weight) and do not contradict the modern vowel-class rule, which Cheung 2018 itself calls 'rhythmic-like.. determined by the quantity/quality of the vowels'.

(2) The classification rests on a 1964 English translation of Abaev's grammatical sketch: a short but primary and authoritative description, and the source every database entry (StressTyp2, Hayes, Hyman) derives from. Glottolog's 'grammar' list is mostly syntax papers; the genuinely fuller descriptions are the Russian reference grammars (Akhvlediani ed. 1963; Bagaev 1965) and the instrumental work of Sokolova 1953 and Dzakhova 2010, all open and downloaded now to ( record there). Each restates the same system: stress confined to syllables 1-2 of the word/accentual

sources.quote: 'The accent is a weak expiratory stress. Word accent is subordinate to phrase accent. In Iron, where an initial i is lost, the first syllable of the group is stressed, although the vowel is short. This happens when the definite article, still preserved in Digor, has been elided ... sources.quote: In the present work a comprehensive account of some important developments which took place in the phonology of that language is given. The developments comprise apocope (loss of final vowel), syncope (loss of medial vowel), aphaeresis (loss of initial vowel), i-epenthesis (insertion of *i) and accompanying palatalization, and finally, the fate of *u. Also the role of the accent in these cases is addressed. (HAL abstract)
